primary_meaning: In Christian teaching, 'Judgment' primarily refers to God's final eschatological judgment: the decisive act at the end of history in which God, exercised through Jesus Christ, holds all humanity accountable, evaluates every person's deeds and relationship to Christ, and renders a verdict that separates the righteous (destined for eternal life) from the wicked (destined for condemnation). It is symbolically depicted through courtroom imagery (books opened, a throne, a verdict), harvest imagery (reaping, winnowing, separating wheat from chaff), and shepherd imagery (separating sheep from goats). The 'Last Judgment' or 'Day of Judgment' is an article of the historic creeds ('he will come again to judge the living and the dead') and is affirmed across Catholic, Orthodox, and Protestant traditions.
primary_basis: Matthew 25:31-46 (the Son of Man separating sheep from goats)
Revelation 20:11-15 (the great white throne; books opened; the dead judged by their works)
2 Corinthians 5:10 (all must appear before the judgment seat of Christ)
Romans 2:5-16 (the day of wrath when God's righteous judgment is revealed; God judges secrets through Christ)
Romans 14:10-12 (we will all stand before God's judgment seat and give account)
Hebrews 9:27 (it is appointed for man to die once, and after that comes judgment)
John 5:22-29 (the Father has given all judgment to the Son; resurrection to life or judgment)
Acts 17:31 (God has fixed a day on which he will judge the world by a man he has appointed)
Matthew 12:36 (account on the day of judgment for every careless word)
Daniel 7:9-10 (the Ancient of Days enthroned, court in session, books opened)
Ecclesiastes 12:14 (God will bring every deed into judgment)
Matthew 13:36-43, 47-50 (harvest and dragnet parables of end-of-age separation)

alternatives.meaning: Temporal or historical judgment within history: God's judgments on nations, cities, and Israel itself through prophetic 'Day of the LORD' oracles, wars, exile, and natural catastrophe (e.g., the flood, Sodom, Babylon, the Assyrian and Babylonian conquests). Much Old Testament judgment language is read this way rather than as end-of-world imagery.
basis: Isaiah 13 (oracle against Babylon)
Amos 5:18-20 (the day of the LORD against Israel)
Ezekiel 7 (judgment on the land of Israel)
Genesis 6-9 and Genesis 19 (flood; Sodom and Gomorrah, cited in 2 Peter 2:4-9 as patterns of judgment)
Nahum and Obadiah (judgments on Nineveh and Edom)

alternatives.meaning: Realized or present judgment: especially in Johannine theology, judgment is already occurring now in people's response to Christ; belief or unbelief constitutes the verdict, and Christ's death is itself the judgment of the world.
basis: John 3:18-19 (whoever does not believe is condemned already; this is the judgment, that light has come into the world)
John 12:31 (now is the judgment of this world)
John 9:39 (for judgment I came into this world)

alternatives.meaning: Judgment as purifying discipline or refinement of God's own people, beginning with the household of God, rather than final condemnation; associated imagery of refiner's fire and testing of works.
basis: 1 Peter 4:17 (judgment begins at the household of God)
1 Corinthians 3:12-15 (works tested by fire; the person saved though as through fire)
Malachi 3:2-3 (refiner's fire, fuller's soap)
Hebrews 12:5-11 (the Lord disciplines those he loves)

alternatives.meaning: A distinct 'bema seat' judgment of believers for rewards, separated in time and purpose from the great white throne judgment of unbelievers; characteristic of dispensationalist systems.
basis: 2 Corinthians 5:10 (judgment seat / bema of Christ)
1 Corinthians 3:12-15 (rewards for works)
Romans 14:10
Revelation 20:11-15 (read as a separate later judgment of the unsaved dead)

alternatives.meaning: Preterist reading: New Testament 'coming judgment' language (especially in the Olivet Discourse and, for full preterists, Revelation) refers principally to the historical judgment on Jerusalem and the temple in AD 70, not (or not only) to a future universal judgment.
basis: Matthew 23:36-24:34 (this generation will not pass away)
Luke 21:20-24 (Jerusalem surrounded by armies)
Matthew 26:64 (coming on the clouds language read as vindication-in-judgment within that generation)

alternatives.meaning: Judgment as human moral discernment and church discipline: the ethical sense in which believers are told not to judge hypocritically yet are to judge rightly and adjudicate matters within the church; a different (non-eschatological) sense of the same term frequently treated in Christian teaching.
basis: Matthew 7:1-5 (judge not, that you be not judged)
John 7:24 (judge with right judgment)
1 Corinthians 5:12-13 and 6:1-5 (judging those inside the church; saints will judge the world)

alternatives.meaning: Judgment with a restorative or annihilationist outcome: universalist readings see judgment as ultimately corrective and reconciling; conditionalist/annihilationist readings see its verdict as final destruction rather than eternal conscious torment. These differ over the result of judgment rather than its reality.
basis: Matthew 10:28 (destroy both soul and body in hell) for annihilationism
1 Corinthians 15:22-28 and Colossians 1:19-20 for universalist readings
2 Thessalonians 1:9 (eternal destruction) contested between views

notes: Judgment is one of the most stable and credal concepts in Christian interpretation: the final judgment of all people by God through Christ is affirmed in the Apostles' and Nicene Creeds and across virtually all traditions, so its core meaning is not disputed. The interpretive diversity concerns scope and timing (final vs. historical vs. already-realized vs. AD 70), the subjects (believers' works vs. unbelievers' condemnation, and whether these are one event or several), and the outcome (eternal punishment, annihilation, or ultimate restoration). Associated symbols consistently attached to judgment include the throne and opened books, harvest/winnowing, fire, scales, the winepress (Revelation 14), and the sheep-goat separation. If the experiment's term intends 'judgment' as a symbol for something else entirely, no such alternative symbolic equation has recognizable consensus; the dominant usage treats judgment as the referent that other symbols (harvest, fire, courtroom) point to, rather than as a symbol standing for a different concept.
